questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. Examination reveals a single, indurated, clean-based ulcer with a cartilaginous feel. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is non-tender and rubbery. Which investigation would be most diagnostic?
opts: Dark field microscopy of serous exudate
questions.exp: The clinical picture is classic primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Dark field microscopy demonstrates motile Treponema pallidum spirochetes from the serous exudate of the ulcer and is the gold standard for diagnosis of primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with multiple, painless, pearly white umbilicated papules on the face. CD4 count is 80 cells/μL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum caused by a poxvirus presents as umbilicated papules. In immunocompromised patients (especially HIV with low CD4), lesions are more numerous, larger (giant molluscum), and facial involvement is characteristic. The umbilicated pearly appearance is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous plaque with sinuses discharging black granules ('grains') on his right foot. Microscopy of the grains shows thick-walled, brown, muriform cells with transverse and longitudinal septa. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (melanin-containing) fungi such as Fonsecaea pedrosoi. The pathognomonic feature is the 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic cells/muriform cells) — thick-walled, brown, septate cells that divide by binary fission in tissue. Black grains in this context are characteristic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of a well-demarcated erythematous plaque with silvery scales on her elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. A skin biopsy shows Munro microabscesses. Which pathological finding best describes this condition?
opts: Neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum
questions.exp: Psoriasis is characterized histologically by Munro microabscesses (neutrophil collections in the parakeratotic stratum corneum), Kogoj spongiform pustules in deeper epidermis, regular epidermal hyperplasia, and dilated dermal papillary vessels. Auspitz sign results from removal of scales exposing these dilated vessels.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man on long-term dapsone therapy for lepromatous leprosy develops acute hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Which enzyme deficiency makes patients most susceptible to this complication?
questions.exp: G6PD deficiency is the most clinically relevant pharmacogenomic risk factor for dapsone-induced hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. Patients with G6PD deficiency have impaired ability to regenerate NADPH, making red cells susceptible to oxidative damage from dapsone metabolites (hydroxylamine intermediates).

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on his trunk. Slit-skin smear shows a bacteriological index (BI) of 0. Nerve biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells but no bacilli. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) represents the high-resistance end of the immunological spectrum. Features: few (1-2) well-defined hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, negative slit-skin smear (BI=0), strong cellular immunity (CMI), well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells reaching up to the dermoepidermal junction, and perineural infiltration.

questions.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on urticarial bases on her trunk and limbs. DIF shows linear deposits of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Which antigen is the primary target?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder. Autoantibodies target BP180 (BPAG2/type XVII collagen, a hemidesmosomal protein) and BP230 (BPAG1). Tense bullae (subepidermal) on urticarial bases, linear IgG+C3 at BMZ on DIF, and elderly patients are classic features. BP180 is the dominant antigen.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with facial erythema in a butterfly distribution, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and polyarthralgia for 3 months. Histopathology of the skin biopsy shows interface dermatitis with vacuolar change, basement membrane thickening, and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. What additional finding on immunofluorescence is most characteristic?
opts: Granular deposits of IgG, IgM, and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction (lupus band test)
Linear IgG at the basement membrane
questions.exp: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) shows the lupus band test on DIF — granular deposits of multiple immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA) and complement (C3) at the dermoepidermal junction. This positive lupus band test in both lesional AND non-lesional (sun-protected) skin is characteristic of SLE. Interface dermatitis is the histological hallmark.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer with chronic sun damage develops a scaly erythematous plaque on his scalp. Biopsy shows full-thickness atypia of keratinocytes with squamous differentiation, without invasion through the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis and malignant potential?
opts: Actinic keratosis — 0.1-0.5% annual risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma per lesion
Bowen's disease — very high risk of invasive SCC in 30% within 5 years
questions.exp: Bowen's disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ (full-thickness epidermal dysplasia). The biopsy showing full-thickness keratinocyte atypia without basement membrane breach confirms SCCIS/Bowen's. Risk of invasive SCC in untreated Bowen's is approximately 3-5% overall, with immunosuppressed patients at higher risk. Actinic keratosis shows partial-thickness atypia.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the left T5 dermatome. She has severe burning pain. Which antiviral drug is the treatment of choice, and what is the primary benefit of early treatment?
opts: Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days — reduces viral shedding and risk of postherpetic neuralgia
Valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for 5 days — eliminates postherpetic neuralgia completely
Famciclovir 250 mg three times daily for 7 days — eradicates latent virus from dorsal root ganglia
Topical acyclovir cream applied 5 times daily — equivalent to systemic therapy
questions.exp: Herpes zoster treatment: oral acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day for 7 days (or valacyclovir 1g TID or famciclovir 500 mg TID for 7 days). Early treatment (within 72 hours of rash onset) reduces severity, duration, and decreases (but does not eliminate) risk of postherpetic neuralgia. Topical therapy is inadequate for zoster.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with a painless, soft, non-tender, compressible genital ulcer with a clean base and no induration. Multiple similar lesions are present. Gram stain shows gram-negative bacilli arranged in a 'school of fish' pattern inside macrophages. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Pathognomonic finding: Donovan bodies — encapsulated intracytoplasmic gram-negative rods within mononuclear cells on Giemsa or Leishman stain of tissue smear, appearing as 'closed safety pin' or 'school of fish'. Lesions are painless, beef-red, easily bleeding granulomatous ulcers.

questions.q: A patient with pemphigus vulgaris is being initiated on systemic corticosteroids. Which of the following best describes the immunopathology of this condition?
opts: IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 causing acantholysis in the suprabasal layer
IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 causing acantholysis in the subcorneal layer
IgA autoantibodies against tissue transglutaminase in dermal papillae
IgG autoantibodies against type XVII collagen at the basement membrane
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and sometimes also desmoglein 1. Binding of antibodies disrupts desmoglein-mediated keratinocyte adhesion, causing suprabasal acantholysis (tombstone row of basal cells). DIF shows intercellular IgG and C3 in a 'chicken wire' pattern throughout the epidermis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with thickened, sclerotic skin on his fingers (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, telangiectasias on the face, and dysphagia for 1 year. What antibody is most associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and is predictive of pulmonary hypertension?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and carries higher risk of interstitial lung disease. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with rapid skin progression and scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. The most likely causative organism and first-line treatment are:
opts: Staphylococcus aureus — topical mupirocin or oral cephalexin
Streptococcus pyogenes — topical fusidic acid or oral amoxicillin
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (and less commonly Streptococcus pyogenes). Classic presentation: honey-colored crusted lesions on face. First-line: topical mupirocin or retapamulin for localized disease; oral cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate for extensive disease. MRSA: TMP-SMX or clindamycin.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a well-demarcated hypopigmented macule with loss of sensation on the left cheek. Slit-skin smear is negative. Lepromin (Mitsuda) test is strongly positive. Wade-Fite stain of biopsy shows no bacilli. Which type of leprosy, and what regimen should be prescribed according to WHO?
opts: Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy — rifampicin 600 mg monthly + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months
Multibacillary (MB) leprosy — rifampicin 600 mg monthly + clofazimine 300 mg monthly + dapsone 100 mg daily for 12 months
Paucibacillary leprosy — dapsone monotherapy for 2 years
Multibacillary leprosy — rifampicin + ofloxacin + minocycline (ROM) single dose
questions.exp: A negative SSS, positive Mitsuda test, and absence of bacilli on Wade-Fite stain indicate paucibacillary (TT/BT) leprosy. WHO PB MDT: rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + dapsone 100 mg daily (unsupervised) for 6 months. MB MDT adds clofazimine and extends to 12 months.

questions.q: A 45-year-old construction worker presents with an indurated, violaceous, nodular plaque on his left leg that developed after minor trauma 6 months ago. KOH preparation of biopsy material shows brown, thick-walled, septate sclerotic bodies with transverse and longitudinal divisions. Culture yields slow-growing black colonies. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis treatment: itraconazole (200-400 mg/day for months to years) is the drug of choice for most cases. Terbinafine is an alternative. Combination itraconazole + terbinafine is used for refractory cases. Cryotherapy and surgical excision are adjuncts for small lesions. Amphotericin B is used for systemic mycoses, not chromoblastomycosis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias and central ulceration (rodent ulcer) on his left cheek. He has a long history of sun exposure. Which feature most reliably distinguishes this from squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: Peripheral palisading of tumour cells with stromal retraction artifact on histology
Presence of keratin pearls and individual cell keratinization
Rapid doubling time with lymphatic spread
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is histologically characterized by islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading of nuclei and stromal retraction artifact (clefting between tumor nests and stroma). SCC shows keratin pearls, individual cell dyskeratosis, and lacks palisading. BCC rarely metastasizes despite local invasion.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with a widespread rash of the trunk after a course of ampicillin for a sore throat. Examination reveals a morbilliform (maculopapular) eruption. What was the likely underlying infection and mechanism?
opts: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — immune complex-mediated drug-virus interaction causing ampicillin rash in 80-100% of EBV cases
Streptococcal pharyngitis — type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to penicillin
Rubella — viral exanthem mimicking drug reaction
CMV — direct cytopathic effect on keratinocytes
questions.exp: Aminopenicillin rash in EBV/infectious mononucleosis is a classic phenomenon — nearly 80-100% of EBV-infected patients develop a morbilliform rash when given ampicillin or amoxicillin. Mechanism: immune complex formation between drug and EBV-related antigens. This is NOT a true penicillin allergy and patients can tolerate penicillin later.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate develops progressive, thickened, lichenified plaques in the antecubital fossae, popliteal fossae, and wrists. She reports severe pruritus since childhood and has asthma. What is the pathophysiology?
opts: Th2-mediated immune dysregulation with IL-4, IL-13 and IL-31 overexpression causing defective skin barrier (filaggrin mutation)
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (AD) pathophysiology: primary Th2 skewing leads to IgE class switching, IL-4/IL-13 suppression of filaggrin and loricrin (barrier proteins), and IL-31-mediated pruritus. Filaggrin (FLG) loss-of-function mutations are the strongest genetic risk factor. Chronic lichenification results from repeated scratching and superimposed Th1/Th17 response.

questions.q: During a Tzanck smear of a vesicle from a patient with suspected herpes simplex infection, you observe giant multinucleated keratinocytes with nuclear molding and margination of chromatin. Which stain is used, and what is the sensitivity of this test?
opts: Giemsa or Wright stain — sensitivity approximately 50-75% for HSV/VZV
PAS stain — sensitivity >95% for diagnosing herpes
Ziehl-Neelsen stain — used for all viral vesicular lesions
questions.exp: Tzanck smear: the vesicle base is scraped, smeared on a glass slide, and stained with Giemsa, Wright, or Papanicolaou stain. Acantholytic, multinucleated giant cells (herpes cells) with nuclear molding and margination are characteristic of HSV and VZV (cannot differentiate between them). Sensitivity ~50-75%; PCR is more sensitive and specific.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunocompetent man presents with a thorn-prick injury on his hand 6 weeks ago, followed by nodular lesions tracking up the lymphatic vessels of the forearm. What organism and pattern of spread is described?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus) classically presents with the lymphocutaneous pattern (sporotrichoid spread): primary nodule at inoculation site followed by ascending nodular lymphangitis along lymphatic channels. Rose thorn, sphagnum moss, and cat scratches are classic vectors. Treatment: itraconazole 100-200 mg/day for 3-6 months.

questions.q: A patient on biologics for psoriasis develops a paradoxical psoriasiform eruption. Which class of biologic is most commonly associated with paradoxical psoriasis?
questions.exp: Paradoxical psoriasis is most commonly triggered by TNF-alpha inhibitors. The mechanism: TNF blockade leads to unopposed type I interferon signaling (pDC-derived IFN-alpha), driving plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce IFN-alpha which promotes psoriasis pathogenesis. Palmoplantar pustular psoriasis is the most common paradoxical reaction pattern.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a chancre on the cervix noted incidentally. VDRL is reactive at 1:8. She is 12 weeks pregnant. What is the treatment and rationale for choosing it?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose — crosses placenta to treat fetal infection; doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy
Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days — preferred in penicillin-allergic pregnant women
Azithromycin 2g single dose — equivalent to penicillin and safe in pregnancy
Ceftriaxone 1g IM daily for 10 days — best fetal penetration
questions.exp: Pregnant women with syphilis should be treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM (single dose for primary/secondary/early latent; 3 weekly doses for late latent). Penicillin is the only proven treatment that crosses the placenta adequately to prevent/treat congenital syphilis. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. Azithromycin has documented macrolide resistance and is NOT recommended.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with a linear, migratory, serpiginous track on the dorsum of her right foot. She returned from a beach holiday in Goa 1 week ago. What is the causative organism and treatment?
opts: Ancylostoma braziliense (dog/cat hookworm) — cutaneous larva migrans; treated with albendazole 400 mg/day for 3-7 days or ivermectin 200 μg/kg single dose
Strongyloides stercoralis — larva currens; treated with ivermectin
Toxocara canis — visceral larva migrans; treated with albendazole
Ancylostoma duodenale — human hookworm; treated with mebendazole
questions.exp: Cutaneous larva migrans (CLM, 'creeping eruption') is caused by animal hookworm larvae (most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense) that penetrate human skin but cannot complete migration. The serpiginous, pruritic, advancing track (2-3 cm/day) is pathognomonic. Treatment: albendazole 400 mg/day for 3-7 days or ivermectin 200 μg/kg single dose (both equally effective).

questions.q: A patient presents with targetoid skin lesions with concentric zones, bullae, and involvement of two mucosal surfaces after starting co-trimoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Temperature is 38.5°C. SCORTEN score indicates 10% mortality risk. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: SJS: detachment of <10% of body surface area (BSA), involvement of ≥2 mucosal surfaces, targetoid/atypical lesions, triggered most commonly by drugs (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs). Erythema multiforme has typical target lesions and is mainly post-infectious (HSV). TEN: detachment >30% BSA. SJS-TEN overlap: 10-30% BSA.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with purpuric papules and plaques on the lower legs, arthralgias, and microscopic hematuria after an upper respiratory infection. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on DIF. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is characterized by the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement, with IgA deposits in vessel walls on DIF. It commonly follows upper respiratory tract infections, especially in children and young adults. LCV with IgA on DIF is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a punch biopsy on a 4mm lesion on the lower back. Which layer of the skin contains the mast cells, fibroblasts, and blood vessels that are relevant in inflammatory dermatoses?
questions.exp: The dermis is divided into papillary (superficial, loose collagen, capillaries, nerve endings) and reticular (deeper, dense collagen, larger vessels, adnexal structures). Mast cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, and the vascular network are predominantly in the dermis. Knowledge of this architecture is critical for interpreting inflammatory infiltrate patterns on biopsy.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with vitiligo is being considered for narrowband UVB phototherapy. Which mechanism best explains NB-UVB's therapeutic effect in vitiligo?
opts: Stimulates melanocyte migration from the hair follicle outer root sheath, induces melanogenesis, and has immunosuppressive effects on T-cell infiltrate
Directly kills T-cells attacking melanocytes by inducing apoptosis through DNA double strand breaks
Upregulates filaggrin expression, restoring skin barrier function
Inhibits JAK-STAT pathway signaling in keratinocytes
questions.exp: NB-UVB (311 nm) treats vitiligo by: (1) stimulating melanocyte stem cells in the outer root sheath of hair follicles to proliferate and migrate to the depigmented epidermis, (2) inducing melanogenesis through MSH/ACTH release, and (3) immunosuppressive effects (reducing CD8+ T-cell infiltrate that destroys melanocytes). Best repigmentation occurs in perifollicular pattern first.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with rapidly growing vegetating nodules on sun-damaged skin of the face. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous epithelium with central keratin-filled crater and overhanging edges. The lesion began 6 weeks ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, self-involuting epithelial tumor arising from the pilosebaceous unit. It typically grows rapidly over 4-8 weeks, stabilizes, then involutes over months leaving a scar. Histology: crater-shaped with central keratin plug, overhanging 'lip' of epidermis, well-differentiated squamous cells with glassy cytoplasm. Considered by many to be a variant of well-differentiated SCC.

questions.q: A Wood's lamp examination is performed on a patient with scalp ringworm (tinea capitis). A bright green fluorescence is noted. Which organism is responsible for this fluorescence pattern?
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UVA): Microsporum species cause bright green/yellow-green fluorescence in tinea capitis (endothrix does not fluoresce). Microsporum canis (zoophilic, from cats/dogs) and M. audouinii (anthropophilic) cause ectothrix infection. Trichophyton species (most common cause of tinea capitis worldwide including T. tonsurans) do NOT fluoresce under Wood's lamp.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with crusted nodules on the scalp, seborrheic areas, and axillae with oral mucosa involvement. Biopsy shows acantholytic cells in the subcorneal layer with neutrophilic infiltrate forming subcorneal bullae. Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells. Desmoglein 1 antibodies are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pemphigus foliaceus (PF): acantholysis in the subcorneal/granular layer (unlike PV's suprabasal acantholysis). Autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 only (not DSG3), so mucous membranes are SPARED (DSG3 is crucial for mucosal integrity). Presents as crusted/scaly lesions in seborrheic distribution. Fogo selvagem is the endemic variant from Brazil.
